archetype.name: Playoff Team (goaltending-first)
archetype.definition: A club whose two goalies and penalty kill are turning a below-water share of the puck into one of the league's stingiest goals-against marks, good enough to sit near the top of the Metropolitan if the saves hold up even partly.

report.headline: Elite saves and a lockdown kill are covering for a team that's getting outshot
report.take:
Ten games in, the Rangers look like a top-ten team on the site (7th of 32) and sit second in the Metropolitan at 6-3-1. They are pacing for 107 standings points, which would be a sharp turnaround from the 85 and 77 of the last two seasons. The record isn't a fluke of close games: Pts vs Goal Diff sits at -0.5, so the standings, if anything, slightly undersell the margin. The margin itself, though, comes almost entirely from one end of the ice.

This is a goaltending-and-kill team. Igor Shesterkin and Dylan Garand have split the starts evenly and both sit at a .927 save percentage, against a league average of .893. Together they are fifth in Goalies GSAx at 6.8. The penalty kill is second in the league at 93.5%, well above the .79 league mark. Behind that, the Rangers allow the 3rd-fewest goals a game. At 5-on-5 they control only 46% of the shot attempts (24th) and get 23.5 shots on goal a game (28th). Their xGF % of .495 says the chances are roughly even, not tilted their way. The offense (23rd by goals a game) is ordinary, and on the power play it is league-average at 20%.

The numbers hide how much rides on percentages. The all-situations PDO of 104.2 ranks 5th, and nearly all of that is save percentage; team shooting at 11.5% is only a touch above league. On the scoring side, Alexis Lafrenière has 7 goals on 19 shots, a finishing rate no one keeps up. Pavel Dorofeyev leads the forwards with 30 shots for just 2 goals and a -7. History says this formula can work in New York: the 2021-22 team posted 110 points with a .471 xGF % on the back of 23.4 GSAx. But those teams banked on one goalie being elite for 82 games. Two goalies at .927 is not a baseline.

Where it heads depends on how gently the save percentage comes down. Fox (9 assists), Lafrenière and a forward group graded A- give the team enough to stay a playoff club. The shot deficit means a regression in goaltending lands straight on the goals-against column. Expect the goals-against rank to slide from elite toward good, and the points pace to cool into the high 90s. That is still a postseason team in this division, but not the juggernaut the pace implies.

strengths.title: Two goalies stopping nearly everything
strengths.body: Shesterkin and Garand each carry a .927 save percentage over five starts. The team's 6.8 GSAx ranks 5th, against a league average of 0.8, and earns the group its A+ grade. It is the backbone of the 3rd-ranked goals-against rate. Some of it is talent, especially Shesterkin's 4.9 GSAx, but two goalies both at this level over ten games will fade toward their norms.

strengths.title: Penalty kill near the top
strengths.body: At 93.5% the kill ranks 2nd, far above the .79 league average. It also lines up with the goaltending, since save percentage props up every kill. No recent Rangers team has killed better than .845, so expect it to drift down, though staying above average is reasonable.

strengths.title: Defense limits volume too
strengths.body: This isn't only goaltending: the Rangers allow 23.2 shots a game, 8th-fewest. Their forwards hold opposing forwards to the 2nd-largest shortfall against expectation, led by wingers held furthest under in the league. The structure keeps the shot count down even when the puck is in their end, and that part should travel.

concerns.title: Losing the puck-possession battle
concerns.body: A 46% CF % (24th) and 23.5 shots a game (28th, 3.7 below league) mean the Rangers spend a lot of time defending. The xGF % of .495 shows the chances against aren't dangerous enough to sink them. But they also aren't creating an edge to fall back on when saves dry up. This shot-share profile has persisted for years, so it is who they are.

concerns.title: PDO this high usually fades
concerns.body: An all-situations PDO of 104.2 ranks 5th, against a league mark of 100.6. Almost all of it is save percentage rather than shooting. When it normalizes, the goals-against rate rises, and the last five games already show more goals allowed than the season rate.

concerns.title: Scoring leaning on Lafrenière's finish
concerns.body: Lafrenière's 7 goals on 19 shots lead the team, and he ranks 6th among left wings. That finishing rate won't hold. Meanwhile Dorofeyev has 2 goals on a team-high 30 shots, and Laba has a .391 xGF % in nearly 15 minutes a night. With the offense 23rd by goals a game, the scoring needs to spread out.

trend.note: The Rangers opened October with four straight wins and have kept points coming since, 7-2-1 over the last ten. But the last five show a looser team defensively, including a 1-7 loss at New Jersey, even as the record holds.

weekAhead.headline: Two road tests in Canada, then a reeling Kings team
weekAhead.body:
The week opens away, which matters: the 1-3 at Washington, 1-7 at New Jersey and 0-1 overtime loss at Columbus all came on the road. Toronto (21st on the site) is the dangerous one on special teams, with a 26.7% power play and the league's best kill. But it allows 29.2 shots a game (26th) behind a D- blueline, so this is a rare game where the Rangers should get volume. Ottawa is 6-3-0 but 16th on the site. Its record leans on close games (Pts vs Goal Diff 1.6, 4th), it scores 25th-best and its 12.8% power play is 27th, the kind of opponent this goaltending tends to smother.

The homecoming against Los Angeles is the best spot of the week. The Kings are 0-4-2 and 31st on the site, with a .619 kill and an F in goaltending. They still out-attempt opponents (52% CF %, 29.8 shots a game), so this isn't a team to sleep on, just one whose goalies are giving games away. Four or more points from the three games is a reasonable expectation.

keyMatchups.title: Rangers kill vs Leafs power play
keyMatchups.body: Toronto's 26.7% power play ranks 7th and runs into the Rangers' 93.5% kill, 2nd in the league. With the Leafs' own kill at a league-best 96.4%, special teams could decide that game. Whichever unit blinks first likely swings it.

keyMatchups.title: Lafrenière against Ottawa's soft wings
keyMatchups.body: Ottawa allows wingers almost a full point a game above expectation (rank 27). Wingers take 49.2% of the points scored against it, well above the league's 37.9%. That sets up well for Lafrenière, Perreault and Cuylle on the flanks.

keyMatchups.title: Power play vs a broken Kings kill
keyMatchups.body: Los Angeles kills just 61.9% of penalties (31st) and saves .861 overall (30th). A Rangers power play running at league average should find chances to pad the margin at home.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the Rangers can win the shot count against Toronto's porous blueline, or once again need their goalie to steal the road game.

restOfSeason.body:
The parts that should last are the shot suppression, Shesterkin's quality and a forward and defense group that both grade A-. The parts that won't are a .927 team save percentage across two goalies, a 93.5% kill and Lafrenière scoring on more than a third of his shots. The 107-point pace assumes all of it holds. A more honest landing spot has the goals-against rate sliding from 3rd toward the top ten and the save percentage settling around .910. That leaves a team in the mid-to-high 90s in points.

Nothing in the sheet suggests the shot-share problem is going away; this franchise has lived below 50% in xGF % for five straight seasons. So the ceiling depends on Shesterkin carrying a heavier, higher-quality share of the starts. That outcome would still fit a playoff team in a Metropolitan where only Carolina is clearly ahead.
swingFactors: How far the team save percentage regresses
Whether shot share at 5-on-5 climbs toward 50%
Secondary scoring beyond Lafrenière and Fox

confidence.note: Ten games, with the record propped up by save percentage and a hot kill.
